title: Qibla Direction Finder: Bearing to the Kaaba
description: Find the qibla bearing from any location with the Qibla Direction Finder — the great-circle direction to the Kaaba, in degrees from true north. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, from New York the qibla bearing is 58.5° — northeast, not southeast — because the shortest path to Mecca crosses the Atlantic toward the sunrise side of the compass rose's north.
quick_answer: The Qibla Direction Finder computes the initial great-circle bearing from your location to the Kaaba in Mecca (21.4225° N, 39.8262° E) — the direction faced in prayer. Enter or detect your location and read the bearing from true north, ready to apply with a compass or phone.

body.t: Home, hotel, airport, campsite — the bearing depends only on where you stand. In New York it is 58.5°; in London 119.0°; the finder computes yours rather than your guessing from a wall chart.
A musalla or home prayer corner gets its qibla line once, accurately — mark it from the computed bearing instead of inheriting a previous occupant's guess.
Historical mihrabs sometimes follow older conventions (cardinal directions, or the Kaaba's own wall axes). The computed great-circle bearing is the modern reference to compare them against.
From North America the qibla points northeast — over the Atlantic, not across the Pacific. The
shows the same geometry for any destination.

On a flat map Mecca looks southeast of New York. On the sphere, the shortest path arcs north-east — initial bearing 58.5° — crossing the Atlantic. Flat-map intuition fails here precisely because the Earth is round, and this finder exists to replace the intuition.

London 119.0° (southeast, as intuition expects), Paris 119.2°, Berlin 136.7°. Europe is close enough to Mecca that flat and spherical intuitions nearly agree — distance 2,566 to 2,979 miles rather than New York's 6,404.

faq: Why do some mosques face a different direction?

Communities have used several conventions across history — great-circle computation, rhumb lines, and cardinal approximations among them. This finder reports the great-circle (shortest-path) bearing, the method most contemporary authorities and apps use; local practice remains a matter for your community.

The bearing is from true north. Magnetic declination varies by place and year (roughly 13° west in New York, near 0–1° east in London at present), so a physical compass reading must be corrected by the local value from a current declination chart.
The spherical computation is precise to well under a degree for any location — far finer than a phone compass or hand compass can be held. Instrument error, not geometry, is the practical limit.
Within the city, direction is toward the Kaaba itself rather than a computed bearing; inside the Grand Mosque, you face it directly. The finder is for everywhere else on Earth.
The antipode of the Kaaba lies in the South Pacific near French Polynesia; from there every direction is qibla. Everywhere else, one great-circle direction is the answer this page computes.
Does the bearing change as I travel?
Continuously — it is a function of your position alone. A long flight crosses many qibla bearings, which in-flight entertainment maps quietly recompute.
Use this page for the number and the phone to apply it — and hold the phone away from metal and magnets, calibrating with the figure-eight motion, since phone magnetometers are easily fooled indoors.
